html:
Krišjānis Barons was a Latvian writer and folklorist who gathered the dainas, the short four-line Latvian folk songs, into a great collection published from 1894 to 1915.

He was a leader of the Young Latvians, who in the mid 1800s argued that Latvians, then peasants under German landlords, were a nation with their own culture. People across the country sent in songs, and Barons sorted more than two hundred thousand texts in a famous cabinet of small drawers, now kept in Riga.

The dainas, about work, nature, family and the old gods, became the treasure of Latvian identity. They were sung at the Song Festivals that began in 1873 and gave words to the Singing Revolution. Compare the Estonian Kalevipoeg and the Finnish Kalevala. See Latvia.
